utterances.text: Would you please now turn to page -- to tab 34. Look at the document from the information centre of Dubrovnik. Page 1 is in English. Please turn to pages 2 and 3, which contains documents in B/C/S. Is it correct that in the translation into English the information at the top of these documents is missing, showing the telephone numbers, the word "Zagreb," the word "Staff of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Croatia," and the stamp of these two documents. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not on the translation; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at the first document from 1445 hours, the Dubrovnik centre for information, 6th of December, 1991. On the right-hand side there is a stamp and I will read it to you. "Republic of Croatia, Ministry of Defence, 6th of December, at 1500 hours," and then there is a signature. You referred to this institution in your replies as the information centre. Do you know that this is part of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please look at tab 35. The JNA staff from Boka is sending a message to the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff and to Minister Davorin Rudolf. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the third sentence it says that General Kadijevic sent to message to you and to the ECMM in Dubrovnik about undertaking an energetic investigation into our responsibility for these events. And then there is a sentence which says: "General Kadijevic summoned me to Belgrade at 1400 hours, so that today I will not be able to continue negotiations with you." Is this a letter sent by Vice-Admiral Miodrag Jokic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You know about the details of this letter? You're familiar with them, right?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with the details, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: With whom was the agreement made that two JNA officers should come to Dubrovnik to take pictures of the damage?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me the request for that was made, the way I remember it, by Minister Rudolf. He had the contact with and the arrangement with that. And in my opinion, it was a good idea. But the exact person he was in contact with, I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us now look at tab 36. And would you turn to page 2, the B/C/S document allegedly an -- a pierce of information from General Strugar to Minister Rudolf. If you look at the lower part, the bottom part, mentioning dates and times, connected to the faxes, the telephone numbers, is it correct that one cannot see how and when this arrived in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You cannot see it on this document -- I'm sorry, I'll have to look at the original. I'm not sure of all these numbers, but it states down here 1714. I remember when I was informed, I logged it. So we can go back to the log and check when I saw it at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please follow what I am saying. When you said 1714, does it say sent by 3850386? This is a Dubrovnik number. Right?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am -- will not say anything about all these numbers and timings. To the best of my knowledge, it looks like it arrived in Dubrovnik at 1715. But all these numbers is -- that's the best I can say about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you also cannot see from which number this arrived in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe not. There's lots of numbers here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me: In the bottom part you can see that it says number of pages: 01?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then in the upper part of the report where it says 1914, 38361847 this is the extension for Split. And then on the right-hand side you can see the result, okay, pages: 02. Where is the second page of this document and what does it represent?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyway, the correspondence was not for me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At tab 37. Underneath this card it says: "Hotel Argentina Dubrovnik, and Hotel Villa Orsula." Can you tell me who was put up in the Villa Orsula?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know in which rooms people -- persons stayed, so I can't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a separate facility, Hotel Villa Orsula, because it is added here by hand. The regards are being sent from the Hotel Argentina and Hotel Villa Orsula. Do you know where this hotel is?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hotel Argentina and Villa Orsula are sort of the same complex. I think it's even owned by the same people. So it's, as far as I was concerned, the same hotel, Orsula, part of it a bit more luxury than the other part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us now move on to the log contained in this tab, and it refers to the meeting held in Cavtat. 11.24 you entered the following: "Two bursts of MG fire heard from direction north-west, later informed by the local authorities that a ZNG soldier had gone mad because his brother had been killed." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: For there similar incidents previous to this one by members of the ZNG?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the only one I can remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I do apologise, but let us go back just for a moment to this letter, the alleged letter from the previous tab that General Strugar sent to Minister Rudolf. Is it correct that in your logbook referring to the events of the 6th of December at 1714 or 1715, this letter is not entered at all?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll have to go back to the log.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It's in tab 30, the last page.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tab 30, last page, yeah. At 1914 --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about 1714 or 1715. There's no entry in the logbook that a message had been received.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. It was received then or handed over to me at the time, 1925. It was not a communication to me; it was passed to me by the people it was sent to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us go back to the 7th of December, tab 37. Would you please look at the time 1355, meeting commenced. You say: "I insisted that the sentence 'freedom of movement for EC monitors' was included. This was accepted by Admiral Jokic who told that we could go wherever we wanted, (interesting from my point of view)." Does this reflect your thoughts because something like this was never said before?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was interesting to hear it again, because it was very positive in my point of view, very positive.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me ask you: In view of the situation connected with Admiral Jokic, was it interesting to hear this from him personally?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It was interesting for the general situation that we were talking about something which was good talk and positive talk to me.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not the same as in the notes of Ambassador Bondioli, the same thing that General Strugar asked for at the meeting on the 28th of October? Was it not the same request that was made by the JNA on the 14th of November, a meeting that you attended also. We spoke about that document and you made notes. This cannot have been the first time that the JNA made just such a request.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. In your log, in continuation, at 1925, as the time is given, second passage of this entry you say: "If Admiral Jokic accepts our freedom of movement it might mean and should mean that he accepts ECMM teams on JNA side." Admiral Jokic, had he opposed this before?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not -- I cannot remember if he had opposed, but the mere fact of life was that we had no ECMM teams on that side on a permanent basis. And this -- to have that, I have stated before, is very, very important in my way of thinking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have full respect for your way of thinking, but isn't it quite obvious that much earlier before the 7th of December the JNA themselves Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. requested the presence of ECMM monitors on their side? We've just given two examples.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the 14th when the first time I now personally recall that there was this request or suggestion to me, you may recall that we, because of the general situation, had removed the EC monitors from Dubrovnik. Now we are coming back because of the initiative of Minister Rudolf and his colleagues. So the situation had changed, seen from my point of view. Now we are starting on something new after having something, whether it is good or not, removing our people. Now we have a chance to get back and try to do what we are supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, again, you are wasting the time I have at my disposal. The question was whether the JNA made a request before in relation to your explanation as concerns the 14th of November. I will remind you that in Ambassador Bondioli's notes from his first meeting with General Strugar when they first met, it was also stated that a request was made and that it would be helpful for ECMM monitors to also be on the side of the JNA. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please look at tab 38. This is the agreement that was signed stating the following: "I want to know about the JNA side now, that the other side is being represented" -- it's the first paragraph of the page I'm talking about. "The JNA being represented by the supreme command of the armed forces of the SFRY and the supreme command of the armed forced of the SFRY as the highest form of command is represented by Vice-Admiral Miodrag Jokic." Is that correct? You were after all at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the next passage, this is compared to the agreement signed in Geneva by the President of Croatia Franjo Tudjman and the federal secretary for national defence, Veljko Kadijevic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that in the very first sentence of this agreement, both sides agree to fully comply with the cease-fire throughout the areas of Metkovic and Dubrovnik municipalities, respectively?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These forces that were deployed around Dubrovnik, did they stretch as far as Metkovic municipality? Were you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Yes, I believe so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It was also agreed to have a permanent link between the respective commands of the armed forces because of the need to exchange information in order to fully implement the aims of this agreement. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just underneath it says that whoever violates this agreement will be prosecuted by both sides of the agreement and duly inform the other side of any such proceedings being undertaken. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: According to that, the report dated the 9th of December, the assessment of damage in Dubrovnik on the part of the JNA, the report was signed by Admiral Jokic, was this report sent to you in order to notify you that there had been an investigation by the JNA?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've never seen that report before I arrived here in The Hague.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In answer to a question by my learned friend from the Prosecution you said that you had seen this report as early as mid-December 1991.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may remember wrong, but I'm answering to the best of my knowledge right now. I might have seen it that, if I have said so. But right now sitting here I can't remember if I saw it at the time. And maybe my absent-minded -- I don't -- but I have seen it for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, let us not waste time, but all the same. If you look at what items 1, 2, and 3 of this agreement say or items 5, 6, and 7 for that matter dealing with issues related to Dubrovnik. Life and work in Dubrovnik, weapons, and so on. Can we agree that you could hear these things being said by the JNA many times before every time you were in touch with them, roughly speaking, that they were in agreement with these proposals and that the JNA had sent many such requests, even prior to December 1991.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please speak into the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have heard proposals -- proposals of that nature before.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can you just tell me, if you look at the bottom of the document, on behalf of the supreme command of the armed forces of the SFRY the agreement was signed by Admiral Jokic, isn't that correct, which you certified by your own signature on the same document?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you just briefly look at tab 39, please. This is a report of the commission on damages caused to the Dubrovnik Old Town. The document was compiled by the command of the 9th Military Naval Sector, and the document was signed by Vice-Admiral Commander Miodrag Jokic. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This document was forwarded to the deputy federal secretary for national defence, Admiral Stane Brovet, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And we do agree that the federal secretary for national defence at the time was General Veljko Kadijevic, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was informed like that, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just briefly look at the last paragraph, which speaks about the opinion of the commission. The last sentence says: "You cannot identify -- the origin of all the damage cannot be stated with certainty or the perpetrators named because it is obvious that a lot of the damage was not caused by attacks from outside the Old Town centre." I am placing my emphasis on the last portion saying that: "It is obvious that a lot of the damage was not caused by attacks from outside the Old Town centre." Would it be your understanding, then, that much of the damage could be caused by operations of firing from inside the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not my understanding, but I am convinced that the main damage or the damage inside the Old Town came from outside the Old Town. The shelling I had witnessed myself on the 6th.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. Please. Listen to me, please. I am not challenging your views on the matter. I am merely asking you the following: What would be your understanding of this specific sentence when Admiral Jokic says: "It is obvious that a lot of the damage was not caused by attacks from outside the Old Town centre." In your understanding, in your interpretation, is it General Jokic's view -- Admiral Jokic's view that the damage was caused by firing or operations inside the Old Town centre? Would that be your interpretation of this sentence?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I was going to object and move to strike that, Your Honour. He's asking this witness for general -- for Admiral Jokic's view. He can't answer as to Admiral Jokic's view. That's a matter for Admiral Jokic when he comes and testifies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That is a fair observation. Mr. Rodic, do you want to try and put the question some other way or will you move on?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was just about to make a link between this and another document that the witness spoke about earlier. It is the letter by General Strugar, which in terms of it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon, the interpreter was interpreting. I'll pause. I think you can accept that the document signed by Admiral Jokic appears to suggest the view that a lot of damage was not caused by attacks from outside the Old Town centre, whatever the admiral may have thought. Now, do you want to go on and deal with another document?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I will. I will now move on and ask the witness to look at tab 36, which is the information report allegedly sent by General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you please look at the last three lines, or rather, four lines when the general says: "Pursuant to my order, the units stopped firing at 11.15 but your forces did not observe a cease-fire. That is why it can be concluded that the buildings in the Old Town are damaged by your forces. My apologies. Your forces have not observed the cease-fire, that is why it can be concluded that the buildings in the Old Town are being damaged by your forces." Does this strike you as a conclusion based on Admiral Jokic's report, or is this similar at least?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, I find it's difficult to see the logic of the last sentences here; it did when I received it. I'm still not sure what -- of the logic of it. And you refer to Admiral Jokic, where he is stating something about --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It reminds me of it, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do agree that there is a similarity between the letter by General Strugar and this report by Admiral Jokic, as concerns the assessment of how the damage in the Old Town came about. Isn't that correct? There are similarities there. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not up to me to decide what the two gentlemen meant. I have no further remarks to this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we please briefly look at tab 41. This is an organisational chart of the JNA in Herzegovina. Do you know where Herzegovina is?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, roughly the borders, yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me roughly where it is.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's pretty close to the Dubrovnik area, if I say so.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you name any town in Herzegovina? Have you ever heard of any town in Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have. Right now I can't remember the towns. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about this organisation chart of the JNA in Herzegovina, what does it belong to? Which forces does it refer to?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who made it, and it -- well, you can -- who does it refer to? The organisation of military units, I guess, in Titograd, Boka, and Titovo. You have the various places where people in units are mentioned, and the various officers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very well. Let us not go any further into this. If you look just where the four X's are, there's a square and inside the square it says "operations group". Just underneath it reads Trebinje and then under that General Strugar --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trebinje is just more or less north of Dubrovnik. I have been there later.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not receiving any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's all very well, but I'm asking you about the square in which it reads: "Operations group," and then underneath "Trebinje" and then further down "General Strugar." During your mission, during your monitoring mission in the former Yugoslavia, did you ever hear any reference to these three terms in -- as belonging to the same context, General Strugar in relation to the operations group or General Strugar in relation to Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, let us please confirm the following: From the 28th of October you were in Split. Isn't that correct? I'm talking about 1991, of course. Is it not correct that from the 9th of November to the 14th of November you provided a detailed description of your participation in the transport of the Slavija ferry without actually being present in the area at the time -- I mean on the land. Can you just tell me briefly your mission in those days --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: -- between the 9th and the 14th, did it have to do with the transport, with the evacuation of refugees from Dubrovnik and taking them further up the coast to Rijeka and Pula. Was that the focus of your mission in those days?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the start I was sitting in our deputy regional centre in Split receiving, between other things, the reports from Dubrovnik and the requests to have the monitors removed. And then on the 11th, we moved down there, first to be checked in Zelenika, then to go back to pick up people in Dubrovnik, then to go back to Zelenika and to be checked again and have a negotiation with the crisis committee members and the JNA.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please. I know all of that. You've talked about that at length. All I'm asking is about the period of time between the 9th and the 14th of November. Is it true that the focus of your mission was on that ship and that you were not in the Dubrovnik area on land at that time going about your duties. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: My main job was the ship, yes, and the evacuation of people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Is it not true that following your departure for Rijeka on the 14th of November, you no longer received firsthand reports from Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, not until I was back in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I must read this out to you from your statement: "Following my return to Split from Rijeka, I continued to go about my daily tasks. However, from that point to my return to Dubrovnik on the 5th of December, 1991, I did not receive any other firsthand reports from Dubrovnik." This applies to the specific period of time, your return from Rijeka, and the 4th and 5th of December, that's at least what you stated to the investigators.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I misstated before -- I didn't hear -- when I left Dubrovnik, I had no contact with Dubrovnik and what I actually should have said before is when I came back I didn't hear anything about Dubrovnik until I was back in Split, and that was not report from EC monitors because they were not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In relation to your whole mission, your participation in the monitoring mission, your stay in Croatia, is it not true that it was only between the 4th and the 8th of December, 1991, that you were physically present in the Dubrovnik area, your arrival in Dubrovnik, you were there on the 6th when there was shelling; on the 7th you were there at negotiations in Cavtat; on the 8th you made a tour of the town with JNA officers. Afterwards you left Dubrovnik which comprises a total of four days. Is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, you have about 2 minutes of tape left.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be done in a minute, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it not true, Mr. Hvalkof, that in the four days of your actual physical presence in the Dubrovnik area in relation to those four days you testified before this Court giving us a lot of information which relates to the entire two months to events throughout the two months in Dubrovnik area of which you had no direct part.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object, Your Honour. That's a speech. That's for final submissions. That's not a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think it can be answered, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Hvalkof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'll go back and read it again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you can please just answer briefly so we can conclude this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have testified to documents I have been forced to look at, yes, from that period.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My last question to you: Is it not true that throughout your testimony we have ascertained that you have been shown documents in a very selective manner. During your testimony we have observed a number of discrepancies between your statements and facts, have we not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I would object again, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And this time, Mr. Weiner, I would uphold you. This is getting to be a final submission, Mr. Rodic. We look forward to hearing it when the time comes, but not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll withdraw the question, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Very well and that --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and I thank the Chamber for your understanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And I hope you appreciate the very considerable consideration we gave you of time on that cross-examination. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon. Re-examined by Mr. Weiner:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We're almost finished, Mr. Hvalkof. I'd like to ask you about a little -- a few questions concerning some matters which were raised yesterday and today. Now, yesterday when you were questioned, you were asked about the need for sending letters of protest to General Strugar after having received letters of explanation from the JNA offices about Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the work on the roadways. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, did you accept at face value or believe all information that was sent to the ECMM, either yourself or the monitors?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- maybe I'm facing a language problem. If I accepted that it was correct. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Did you accept as correct and true all the different letters sent to the ECMM?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we had to accept it. We are not sitting there to suppose that people are telling us lies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, when things were sent to the ECMM, did you ever receive information from the parties which you disbelieved?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle we didn't disbelieve anything, but of course you as an individual could sit and be a bit doubtful now and then. But it's not up to us to tell people that it was not true what they were telling us. You had in principle, of course, to believe it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that you received a letter which is exhibit -- Defence Exhibit Number 27 from Colonel Svicevic the same person you testified -- that's a Defence Exhibit, not tab 27, sir. The same person who you testified had threatened some ECM monitors. What if any level of trust did you have at the ECMM with Colonel Svicevic?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was clearly -- I was clearly briefed about that this was a man the ECMM members should not talk to because he was threatening people on their lives. I have not met this gentleman myself. I was briefed about it and I have heard monitors who were threatened tell about or inform me that they had been threatened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the fact that the ECMM monitors in Dubrovnik protested to General Strugar that the road work constituted an aggressive act after receiving letters of explanation from the JNA, what does that tell you about the ECMM monitors in Dubrovnik's belief of the JNA explanations?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the EC monitors were, as I said before, passing complaints both ways if they got them. If they got them from JNA, they would pass them to the other people. And of course they had their own evaluation of the situation, so I can only assume - not proved - that they felt it was sort of a threat, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you've indicated that road work can be an aggressive military act under circumstances. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I've experienced that in several other missions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also some discussion, if we move to another subject, about the Crisis Staff and your meetings with the Crisis Staff and the monitors' meetings with the Crisis Staff. Did you or any of the monitors ever observe any Dubrovnik Crisis Staff members carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or any of the ECMM monitors ever hear any of the Dubrovnik Crisis Staff members threatening military action?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean military action against us?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Against you or against the JNA.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not against us. And to the best of my knowledge, not in our presence to the JNA or to us in that respect, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see any crisis, I say, staff, or crisis committee members wearing military uniforms, those members that you knew wearing military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have stated today that on one occasion I believe there was one of the members in something which looked like a uniform, camouflage dress.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did -- was that member armed?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if that was a member of the Crisis Staff or a part of the Crisis Staff's security team, if they have any?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know if that person was a local police officer?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure he was a member of what you could call the delegation of the Croats who showed up, who came with that group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, let's briefly move to another topic. You were questioned yesterday and a bit today about General Strugar and other members of the JNA requesting investigations about incidents or offering ECM monitors to come on to JNA-controlled areas. In fact, you were questioned about that both today and yesterday, about requests to -- for the monitors to come on to JNA areas. During General Strugar's command of the Dubrovnik area or the JNA troops in the Dubrovnik area, did the ECMM monitors have free access to the JNA-controlled areas?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not according to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you visited JNA-controlled areas, did you ever have free access?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you allowed to walk through JNA-controlled areas and freely investigate allegations of shootings?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I want to ask you another question that was raised. They asked you today about firing or shooting in the vicinity of the Argentina Hotel during that period of shelling in November. And you noted it in tab 11. Could you please turn to tab 12, page 4. Now, on tab 12, page 4, it should have the last three digits on the top as 324.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right, I'm there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you please read the notation at -- please read the notation at 1420 hours, which is 2.20 p.m.?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Incident at entrance of hotel." It's made there briefer, but that's the content of the message.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you continue --

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: "A sniper from the slope opposite hotel has shot and wounded four people -- shot at and wounded four people, three hotel employees and a French journalist. All four wounded in legs or feet."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Finally, could you turn to -- actually, you don't even have to turn to the document. Remember Ambassador Van Houten's protest to Colonel Kadijevic on November 10th?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After that protest was issued, did you receive authorisation of any kind to travel to Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just want to -- the date was --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: November 10th.

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. After November 10th, we had this visit -- first visit to pick up the people. And after that, we could not go to Dubrovnik before it was arranged by Minister Rudolf and his colleagues.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, the letter was written to General Kadijevic, and in that letter you complained that -- or Ambassador Van Houten complained - if we can go to document 15 - that General Strugar, commander of the forces in the Dubrovnik area -- or that -- that the issue of the breach of cease-fire had been sent to General Raseta and General Strugar, who was the commander of the forces in the Dubrovnik area, without any response. Did the minister of defence, General Kadijevic, ever respond in the manner that General Strugar was not the commander of the forces in the Dubrovnik area?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have never seen it or heard it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, before you sit, an issue which the Chamber has noticed and which you may wish to take up with the witness is the documents that are exhibit P61, 1 and, I think, 2, but certainly Defence Exhibits D26 and D27, that group of documents. While they appear on the face of it to be documents addressed by different people to others, they all have a remarkable similarity of handwriting style. Is it that these are originals, or are they a copy produced by the one person? I thought I would mention it now in case you may want to take the matter with this witness, if the Chamber is seeing the documents correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness please be shown Documents D25, 26, and 27.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you've heard the Court's question. First let me ask you: In what language are those three documents?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are in English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what language was the messages sent to you?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were normally passed in -- I have to be careful, but let's say in the local language.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And once it's received in the local language, what happens next?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to translate them. For that reason, we had interpreters. In our case, now and then our own people who could, and otherwise we had to rely on interpreters from one of the sides where we were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, the fact that those three letters, those three exhibits, D25, 26, and 27, are in similar handwriting, what if anything does that say to you?

utterances.speaker: PER HVALKOF [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that the same interpreter has been used.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Any further questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner, for clarifying that matter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Hvalkof, may we say, first, your time has come. Secondly, may we thank you for your attendance here and the time you spent. And we wish you well on your journey back to your farm.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. May I thank for kind treatment from Your Honour and Your colleagues, from everybody in this room. I wish you all well, all of you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you then. You are free to go, Mr. Hvalkof.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do I see you, Mr. Kaufman?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: You indeed, Your Honour. Good afternoon. The next witness is Dr. Colin Kaiser. We have half an hour in which to introduce him. There is no way we will finish, unfortunately, the examination-in-chief today. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No apology from you is called for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. So if I may call Dr. Kaiser. Your Honour, I should like to take this opportunity also to introduce Ms. Andrea Matacic, a research officer from the Office of the Prosecutor. She will be assisting me in this matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. If you would be kind enough to take the affirmation which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could be seated. Yes, Mr. Kaufman. Examined by Mr. Kaufman: If it pleases Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Sir, if could you state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: My full name is Colin Reid Erlin Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your age?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: I'm 54 years old.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your current address, please.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: 105 rue Haxo in the 20th district of Paris, France.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Colin Kaiser, could you tell the Court where you acquired your title and in what discipline.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Well, I'm a social and institutional historian of the -- of Old Regime France, by training. My doctorate was a D.Phil. at the University of London, United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And could you give a brief description of your employment from 1985 until today.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: In 1985, I joined the International Council on Monuments and Sites as an assistant to the director. In 1987, I was asked to become the director of the International Council of Monuments and Sites which is a nongovernmental organisation. It works in cultural heritage and works with UNESCO. I was the director of the international secretariat of ICOMOS. In 1991 I was asked by UNESCO to go to Dubrovnik as an observer. After this mission I worked for the parliamentary assembly of the Council of Europe from end of 1992 until the summer of 1994 in Croatia and Bosnia and Herzegovina, working on the questions of the destruction of cultural heritage. In the summer -- no in the fall of 1994 I was asked by UNESCO to return to Mostar in Herzegovina as a consultant working on cultural heritage. I served a series of missions, going back and forth between Mostar and Paris until the summer of 1995, I was asked by UNESCO if I would like to become the representative and head of office, the UNESCO office, in Sarajevo, and I took up that function in October 1995. I returned to headquarters in 1999 where I stayed for a year and four months. I was asked again by UNESCO to return to Sarajevo to be the representative and head of office again, which I was until the closing of the country office in Bosnia-Herzegovina in September 2003. Now I am -- I have been reintegrated into headquarters and I work in the education sector of UNESCO.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. How did it come about that you were specifically requested to travel to Dubrovnik in 1991?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: In the fall in 1991, sometime early in November, I was approached by Professor Leon Pressouyre, who was a consultant who worked on the -- worked for ICOMOS on the world heritage nominations and he asked me if I would be ready, willing to go to Dubrovnik for UNESCO. I said, Yes I would. And then a short while later I was informed that -- I was asked if indeed I would go and I said yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you enlighten us as to UNESCO's particular involvement in Dubrovnik. What was UNESCO concerned about Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: The first thing to keep in mind was Dubrovnik was inscribed on the World Heritage List in 1979 and the world heritage list is constituted under the convention -- the World Heritage Convention and that is a UNESCO convention. So UNESCO does have a kind of stewardship over the sites that are on that list. Also UNESCO had been alerted by the authorities in Dubrovnik that there had been damage done to the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you travelled to Dubrovnik, did you have a specific mandate?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Well, I was engaged on a consultancy contract. Under that contract I was representative but in fact an observer representative because I report directly to the director general. My specific mandate in Dubrovnik in the framework of the world heritage convention and also The Hague Convention 1954 on cultural heritage in time of war was to ascertain if any military damage or damage had been done from military causes to the Old Town of Dubrovnik and also to make recommendations eventually if there was a restoration which would be required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. So at this time it may be appropriate to submit to the Trial Chamber and to you of course as well a bundle of documents which has been prepared containing your exhibits. I believe the bundles have already been supplied to the Trial Chamber. Perhaps if these could be put in front of Your Honours' computer screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Could I ask Mr. Usher -- sorry, Ms. Usher today, if the bundles could be placed in front of the witness as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, could you look at the monitor in front of you, if Ms. Usher could kindly put the monitor on display, video. This is to be found at tab 5 in the bundle. Please have a look at this letter. Do you recognise that letter, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is that letter?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: That is a letter of appointment from the director general of UNESCO to me regarding the mission to Dubrovnik, personal representative and observer.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see the letter, sir, is dated the 20th of November, 1991. When did you set off for Dubrovnik pursuant to that letter?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: We set off to Dubrovnik -- we arrived in Dubrovnik on the 27th of November, but earlier we went to Belgrade and also to Zagreb. So I would have left on mission a few days following the reception of this letter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So out of the two cities that you've mentioned, Belgrade and Zagreb, where was your first port of call?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: The first port of call was Belgrade, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whom did you meet there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: We were taken to have a high-level meeting with federal military and civilian authorities. I remember there was General Pujic at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you aware of General Pujic's position within the hierarchy of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not sure of his exact ranking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, could you tell us what General Pujic said at that meeting.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Well, General Pujic described the general situation that was reigning on the territory of the Republic of Croatia. As the discussion was mainly, however, about Dubrovnik, about the organising of the mission at Dubrovnik, conditions and security, but also the question of the engagements of federal authorities towards Dubrovnik and the security of Dubrovnik. And Mr. -- and General Pujic talked about those various guarantees that the Federal Government was giving.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was present, apart from yourself, at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Mr. Daniel Janicot who was the director of the cabinet. The director general of UNESCO was present with his assistant, Mr. Rok Vogric. And also Mr. Bruno Carnez who was a UNESCO functionary and who was the other observer in the mission, and myself.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the conversation at any point in time turn to the topic of the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Yes. The discussion of course turned to the situation of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was discussed concerning the Old Town of Dubrovnik? I would refer you to General Pujic's comments.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Well, General Pujic pointed out that a guarantee had been given that the Old Town would not be bombarded, although he pointed out that -- he said that mortars had been placed at the foot of the walls, but that the federal army would not respond to any provocations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to interject at this point in time and ask you, sir, as we will later find you indeed were in Dubrovnik. I take it you are familiar with the ramparts and the walls of the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Yes, I'm very familiar with the Old Town and the walls.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have occasion when you were in Dubrovnik to tour the walls of the Old Town of Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Definitely. It was extremely important to go up on the walls. I was on the walls every day practically before the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So bearing in mind General Pujic's statement, what do you have to say about the matter, based upon your tours of the walls in Dubrovnik? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: I didn't see any mortar positions or any military positions at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. We'll come back to that when we discuss the Old Town of Dubrovnik in more detail. But if I can take you back now to the meetings you had prior to your arriving in Dubrovnik. You've talked about the meeting in Belgrade. One last question I'd like to ask you about that: Was this meeting conducted through an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Yes, it was. It was conducted through an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you conversant in B/C/S, sir?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And whose interpreter was this?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: This was an interpreter who was supplied by the federal authorities.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, you mentioned you had a meeting in Zagreb as well or you moved on to Zagreb. Did you have meetings there?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: We had quite a number of meetings, in fact, in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many days after your meeting in Belgrade was that?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: One or two days. I mean, as soon as we got into Zagreb, we began to have meetings.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Does the name Stamenkovic mean anything to you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Stamenkovic, it certainly does because we had a meeting with him, several meetings with him, in fact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell the Trial Chamber about a conversation that you had or a meeting that you had with the said Colonel Stamenkovic, where it was and what was said.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: The meeting with Stamenkovic was held in the headquarters of the 5th Military District in Zagreb. These meetings were about guarantees for travel to Dubrovnik. We also -- we had explained also to the federal authorities what we were doing in Dubrovnik. And my colleague, Mr. Carnez, indicated that we would raise the flags of the United Nations over the Old Town as a form of protection. Colonel Stamenkovic said that federal army would not shoot and that we would even receive a written guarantee to this effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever receive a written guarantee to that effect?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: No, we never received a written guarantee to that effect. When we -- when Mr. Carnez insisted about flags, Colonel Stamenkovic said it was extremely good, it was very important. And if they were flags of peace, to run them up immediately. However, flags are formalities; they are inert forms. I remember him using that expression and flags will not prevent action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Who was present at that meeting, apart from Stamenkovic, and yourself, and Carnez?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: We had an interpreter provided by the Croatian side. General Raseta was, I think, present briefly in the meeting. I think he was the commander of the 5th Military District, but he was not present for this particular exchange that we had with Colonel Stamenkovic. And that was it. It was a very small meeting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So let us turn to Dubrovnik. How and when did you arrive in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: We arrived in Dubrovnik very late in the evening of the 27th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who greeted you?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: We were received at the -- we landed at the Port of Gruz, the new port of Dubrovnik. We were greeted by Mr. Matko Vetma and Mr. Zvonko Franic who were architects from the Institute for the Protection of Cultural Heritage in Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Had you pre-arranged your meeting with these people?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: We had not pre-arranged the meeting with the people. I think it was arranged through Zagreb, through the authorities in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you housed in Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: We were housed in the institute building, obviously for the protection of cultural heritage. It was in the Old Town. It has always been understood that we would actually be in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And where is the institute building situated?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: The institute building is just on the other side of the street from the Dominican monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you arrived there with a mandate from Mr. Federico Mayor, director of UNESCO. How did you go about putting that task -- those tasks contained in the mandate into action? What were the first things that you did?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Well, the very first thing we did and it was morning of the 28th of November, with the officials of the city, we went around and we had three United Nations flags, and we hauled these three flags over the three bastions of the walls of Dubrovnik on Fort Minceta, on the bastion, Fort St. John, and also Fort Bokar. So it was the -- our tour was the very first thing that we did when we got there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe that Fort St. John is also known as St. Ivan?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I wonder at this point in time if we could show you a map and have you point out these places. Okay. On the Elmo, then. Sir, first of all, if you could, point out the institute and the Dominican monastery. In blue pen, please mark.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: This is P13, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's the Dominican monastery.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In you could put the letter A beside that so we have a frame of reference. Thank you. If you could signify where the institute is.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: I'll comment this is not a very good map. The institute is about here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you could just put a line -- an X, perhaps you could put an X.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We'll use that as a frame of reference. Now, without marking, just for the benefit of the Court because they are marked on the map, I do believe. Point out the Minceta St. Ivan's turret and the Boka turret.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: This is Minceta right here and this is Boka right down here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And St. Ivan, please.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: And this is St. John's bastion here.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Why did you put the UN flags in those turrets?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: The UN flags were run up over the town as a reminder that the town was protected under The Hague Convention and also the World Heritage Conventions, they're UNESCO conventions. But UNESCO is a United Nations agency.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Hague Convention signs.

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were these in position anywhere in the Old Town?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: There were a certain number of Hague Convention signs which were placed on individual monuments in the Old Town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of monuments were they put on?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: There was a -- there was one flag which was on the Sponza Palace. There was another palace which was on the palace of the rectors. Another one on St. Blaise Church. Another one on the cathedral.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you've told the Court that the first thing you did on the morning of the 28th of November was put up these flags. What did you do immediately thereafter? What was your plan of action?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Well, we had also a certain number of explanatory meetings with the officials of the town. We had a lunch with them. That was to explain to them and there were journalists there as well, but the most important part of my job was to verify whether or not there had been any damage caused to the Old Town in earlier events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "earlier events," to what earlier events are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: There had been apparently shelling of the town on the 23rd of October, and there had been shelling the 10th -- from the 10th to the 12th of November as well. We received information about the shellings earlier. So the question was to simply go and verify them. We had received -- on the spot, we received a small report that had been prepared by the institute. And that would be sort of the base -- some base material to see what, in fact, actually happened. But the important thing was to actually go and see what had happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So how would you physically go about verifying the damage that had allegedly been caused, as you say, in October and November?

utterances.speaker: COLIN KAISER.
utterances.text: Well, of course the question was to go physically on to the sites, which is something I did. Sometimes I was accompanied by Mr. Carnez. The -- we had to sort of -- first of all, we had to verify the information that was put into their report. It quickly transpired, though, that I had to find a better tool, a better methodology, in order to summarise and to present the damage. And that was something I began to work on very, very rapidly, I think, on the afternoon even of the 28th of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Kaiser.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point in time I would like to cease the examination-in-chief because I see we are approaching the appointed time for conclusion of the hearing today. I have a wish to express to Your Honours as well. The fact that I will be presenting a number of exhibits tomorrow to the witness, and instead of presenting exhibits now with only a couple of minutes remaining, I think it would be appropriate to do so tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kaufman. Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Defence of General Strugar would like to ask leave to address you on two topics tomorrow morning. We do not want to say when that might be convenient for the Chamber, either before the beginning or at the end of tomorrow's session. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, Mr. Petrovic, what those two issues are.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, yes, I can. As you may assume, one of these topics is the Doctor's report, which I believe has already reached Your Honours. And the second topic is connected to the trial schedule. And we would only address you for ten minutes on those two topics, if you would allow me to address you briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Can I indicate, Mr. Kaufman, as you're on your feet that we would plan to take up with you tomorrow the question of the -- any medical examination of the accused that is contemplated and the timetable for that and pursuing the Defence motion as to the health and the continuance of the trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour. I will pass the message along and I'm sure that the relevant attorney who will deal with the matter will be present in court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. I think it may be convenient for that to be dealt with that at the beginning of the day, I would think, so as to give Dr. Kaiser's evidence a clear run.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAUFMAN
utterances.text: As Your Honour pleases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will adjourn until tomorrow. I must ask you to return in the morning, Dr. Kaiser. Thank you.
